claims.text: The as-built Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy is additively manufactured and has an fcc matrix.
The as-built alloy contains residual stresses and microstructural features characteristic of rapid solidification.
High-temperature degradation in both oxidizing and reducing environments is governed by selective oxidation of Cr and, to a lesser extent, Al.
Selective oxidation forms a brittle, poorly adherent Cr-rich oxide scale.
In oxidizing gases, the Cr-rich scale grows and subsequently spalls during thermal cycling.
In reducing environments, insufficient oxygen destabilizes or prevents formation of a coherent protective scale.
Failure or absence of the protective scale leads to internal oxidation and elemental redistribution.
Internal oxidation and elemental redistribution cause microstructural embrittlement that can trigger catastrophic failure.
Controlled pre-oxidation can form a thin, uniform, adherent Cr2O3 surface layer.
The integrity and adherence of the preformed Cr2O3 scale control subsequent oxidation and scaling dynamics.
Thermal cycling or reducing conditions can cause the Cr-rich scale to spall or fail to form properly.
Scale failure exposes the alloy to rapid internal oxidation and microstructural degradation.
Pre-oxidized specimens will have a more stable and adherent Cr2O3 scale than untreated specimens.
Pre-oxidation will reduce scale spallation relative to the untreated baseline.
Pre-oxidation will reduce internal oxidation and grain-boundary degradation relative to the untreated baseline.
Pre-oxidation will improve retention of mechanical properties after high-temperature exposure.
Untreated as-built specimens rapidly form unstable scales that spall and cause early catastrophic failure in oxidizing or reducing environments.
The proposed mechanism applies primarily to sustained exposure above approximately 900°C when oxygen availability controls oxidation kinetics.
The mechanism may not govern at lower temperatures or when other degradation mechanisms dominate.
The kinetics of oxide formation and spallation and the relative effect of oxidizing versus reducing conditions remain uncertain.

contradictions.description: The account attributes degradation in a nominally reducing atmosphere to the absence of oxygen while also predicting rapid internal oxidation. Internal oxidation requires a nonzero oxygen potential, so the proposed sequence is internally incomplete unless residual oxygen, water vapor, or another oxygen source is specified.
